method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia in children.** In infants and toddlers it is mainly nutritional (too few iron-rich foods or too much cow milk), rarely malabsorption or GI bleeding. **Transfusion is rarely required.**
claims.source_text: Iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia in children Iron deficiency in infants and toddlers is predominantly a nutritional disorder (insufficient iron-rich foods or excessive cow milk consumption) and is rarely due to malabsorption or gastrointestinal bleeding Blood transfusion is rarely required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors** (the page tabulates them across infants, children and adolescents; column split not restated here): maternal iron deficiency, prematurity/low birth weight, multiple pregnancy, exclusive breast-feeding after 6 months, late or insufficient iron-rich solids, excess cow milk, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, vegetarian/vegan diet, GI disorders (e.g. Meckel diverticulum, coeliac, IBD), other chronic blood loss, **heavy menstrual bleeding**, extreme athletes.
claims.source_text: Risk factors for iron deficiency Infants Children Adolescents Maternal iron deficiency Prematurity and/or low birth weight Multiple pregnancy Exclusive breast-feeding after 6 months Late or insufficient introduction of iron-rich solids Excessive cow milk consumption Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Vegetarian or vegan diet Gastrointestinal disorders eg Meckel diverticulum, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, gastric or intestinal surgery or infection Other chronic blood loss Vegetarian or vegan diet Heavy menstrual bleeding Gastrointestinal disorders eg coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, gastric or intestinal surgery or infection Other chronic blood loss Extreme athletes
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Symptoms:** impaired cognition, memory, learning and concentration; behavioural disturbance; fatigue; pica.
claims.source_text: Impaired cognitive function, decreased memory, impaired learning and concentration Behavioural disturbance Fatigue Pica
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ferritin <20 μg/L = borderline/low iron stores**; local thresholds may vary (e.g. 10-30 μg/L).
claims.source_text: A ferritin of <20 μg/L indicates borderline/low iron stores. Also refer to local guidance as the ferritin threshold for low iron stores may vary eg between 10-30 μg/L
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **A normal ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency** with coexisting infection, inflammation or liver disease (acute phase reactant).
claims.source_text: Serum ferritin is an acute phase reactant and a normal result does not exclude iron deficiency in the presence of coexisting infection, inflammation or liver disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not request iron studies or serum iron to diagnose iron deficiency** — serum iron reflects recent intake, not stores.
claims.source_text: Iron studies or serum iron should not be requested to diagnose iron deficiency Serum iron reflects recent iron intake and does not provide a measure of the iron stores
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **An FBE is needed to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia** — typically microcytic, hypochromic (low MCV and MCH).
claims.source_text: An FBE is needed to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia (IDA). Most commonly the red blood cells are microcytic and hypochromic (reduced MCV and MCH)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat low ferritin, with or without anaemia, with iron plus dietary change:** more iron-rich foods, less cow milk.
claims.source_text: Iron supplementation and dietary modification for children with low ferritin, with or without anaemia Dietary advice Increase iron-rich foods and reduce cow milk consumption
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **No cow milk under 12 months; limit to <500 mL/day over 12 months.** Consider dietitian referral.
claims.source_text: Cow milk should not be offered to children <12 months and should be limited to <500 mL/day in those older than 12 months Consider referral to a dietitian
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Doses are elemental iron. Prevention: 1-2 mg/kg/day (max 30 mg/day). Treatment of iron deficiency and IDA: 3-6 mg/kg/day**; consider higher doses in severe anaemia (Hb <80 g/L).
claims.source_text: Doses are based on elemental iron content 1-2 mg/kg/day (max 30 mg/day) is the preventative dose for iron deficiency 3-6 mg/kg/day is the recommended dose for treatment of iron deficiency and IDA. Higher doses should be considered in children with severe anaemia (Hb <80 g/L)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **These doses are for infants and children >1 month**; use neonatal guidelines for neonates.
claims.source_text: Dosing below is for infants and children >1 month of age. Refer to local neonatal guidelines for dosing in neonates
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Warn parents:** black stools, constipation and teeth staining — drink through a straw and brush teeth afterwards. Vitamin C (e.g. orange juice) improves absorption.
claims.source_text: Advise parents that iron preparations can make a child’s stool black in colour and may cause constipation Oral iron preparations may also stain a child’s teeth. Consider having the child drink the iron preparation through a straw and brush the child’s teeth following administration Iron is better absorbed if taken with vitamin C eg orange juice
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Never give oral and parenteral iron together; withhold oral iron for at least one week after an infusion.**
claims.source_text: Do not give oral and parenteral iron together. Oral iron should be withheld for at least one week after an iron infusion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severe anaemia: follow up within a week** to check compliance and response (reticulocytosis, rising Hb).
claims.source_text: In children with severe anaemia, early follow up (within a week) should be arranged to ensure compliance and an appropriate response to treatment (reticulocytosis and increase in Hb)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Continue iron for at least 3 months after the anaemia is corrected**, then recheck Hb and ferritin. **Poor compliance is the leading cause of treatment failure.**
claims.source_text: Iron supplements should be continued for a minimum of 3 months after anaemia has been corrected to replenish stores. Hb and ferritin should be checked at this time Assess for any potential issues with compliance, as poor compliance is the leading reason for treatment failure
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Over-the-counter multivitamin/mineral supplements don't contain enough iron to treat IDA — don't use them.**
claims.source_text: Over the counter multi-vitamin or minerals supplements do not contain sufficient iron to treat iron deficiency anaemia and should not be used
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ferrous sulfate oral mixture (Ferro-liquid®) = 6 mg/mL elemental iron.** Iron polymaltose mixture (Maltofer®) = 10 mg/mL, for children who don't tolerate Ferro-liquid; off-label under 12 years.
claims.source_text: Elemental iron content Notes Ferrous sulfate oral mixture Ferro-liquid® 6 mg/mL … Iron polymaltose mixture Maltofer® 10 mg/mL May be appropriate for children who do not tolerate Ferro-liquid Off-label use for children <12 years old
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Fefol® spansules (ferrous sulfate 270 mg) = 87.4 mg (elemental iron column)**; can be opened and sprinkled on food, not crushed or chewed. **Ferro-grad® (ferrous sulfate 325 mg) = 105 mg** (same column), modified release, swallowed whole.
claims.source_text: Ferrous sulfate delayed release capsules or spansules (270 mg) Fefol® 87.4 mg Spansules can be opened and the beads sprinkled on food to give lower doses They should not be crushed or chewed … Ferrous sulfate (325 mg) tablet Ferro-grad® 105 mg Modified release tablet May be appropriate for older children who can swallow whole tablets
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild to moderate IDA (3 mg/kg/day), Ferro-Liquid:** <10 kg 0.5 mL/kg/day · 10 kg 5 mL/day · 20 kg 10 mL/day · 30 kg 15 mL/day · >40 kg 20 mL/day.
claims.source_text: Mild to moderate IDA - to provide 3 mg elemental iron/kg/day Weight Ferro-Liquid Fefol® spansules Ferro-grad® modified release tablets <10 kg 0.5 mL/kg/day NA NA 10 kg 5 mL per day Half a spansule 5 days/week NA 20 kg 10 mL per day One spansule 5 days/week NA 30 kg 15 mL per day One spansule daily 1 tablet daily >40 kg 20 mL per day

claims.claim: **Over 40 kg,** doses are usually limited to one spansule/tablet per day unless Hb and reticulocytes fail to improve.
claims.source_text: Note: doses in children >40 kg are usually limited to one spansule/tablet per day unless no improvement in Hb and reticulocyte count
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider IV iron for:** contraindication, intolerance or serious compliance problems with oral iron · malabsorption (e.g. GI disease) · erythropoietin-stimulating agents · blood loss exceeding absorptive capacity · rapid repletion (e.g. before non-deferrable surgery) · persistent deficiency despite a 3-month oral trial.
claims.source_text: Contraindications to oral iron or serious issues with compliance or tolerance Comorbidities affecting absorption eg gastrointestinal disease Children receiving erythropoietin-stimulating agents Ongoing blood loss that exceeds the body’s iron absorptive capacity Requirement for rapid iron repletion eg preoperatively for non-deferrable surgery Persistent iron deficiency despite adequate oral therapy (3-month trial)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the local paediatric team** if the cause is unclear or deficiency persists despite a 3-month adequate oral trial.
claims.source_text: Cause of iron deficiency is unclear Persistent iron deficiency despite adequate oral therapy (3-month trial)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Iron deficiency' (Last updated Aug 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Iron_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23
